Some notes from me (Ines)

Pictures I have:
- about 60 photos of dishes and the jar wall, taken by Priya Nair for the
  restaurant's website
- my own phone photos of the larder, labels and all
- scans of all four issues of Brine (drawings by my friend Olu)
- a photo of my grandmother's ogiri pot

Things people ask me about: the jar wall, the koji room (it is a cupboard),
the staff meal, and the workshops I run on the first Monday of the month.

I took over the kitchen in September 2022.

Books that got me here: The Art of Fermentation by Sandor Katz, and Wild
Fermentation. And my grandmother, who never measured anything.
(Saved from LinkedIn as text, October 2026)

Ines Okafor
Head Chef at Saltmarsh. Fermentation, whole-vegetable cooking, apprentices.
Leeds, England, United Kingdom

ABOUT
I cook at Saltmarsh, a 40-seat restaurant in Leeds. Most of what I care about
happens before service: what we do with the trim, the whey, the stems and the
bones. We have a wall of jars and a prep list that is longer than the menu.
I run our apprentice programme and write a small zine about preserving,
called Brine.

EXPERIENCE

Head Chef, Saltmarsh, Leeds
Mar 2022 to present
- A menu that changes every week
- Cut kitchen food waste from 14 kg to 5 kg a week
- Built the larder: 40+ ferments, vinegars and garums on rotation
- Two apprentices a year since 2023

Sous Chef, The Corn Exchange Kitchen, Leeds
Jun 2019 to Feb 2022
- Ran the pass on a 90-cover service
- Took over ordering and brought the supplier list from 31 to 12

Chef de Partie, Brassica, Manchester
Sep 2016 to May 2019
- Larder and garnish, then sauce

Fjaerland Fermentation Lab, Norway
Jan 2018 to Mar 2018

EDUCATION
Leeds Kitchen College. Diploma in Professional Cookery, 2014 to 2016

VOLUNTEERING
Sunday Pot, Leeds. Co-founder. 2021 to present
A hot meal every Sunday at St Aidan's hall, cooked from what restaurants in
the city have left over.

PUBLICATIONS
Brine. A zine about preserving. Four issues, 2022 to 2025.

RECOMMENDATIONS
Callum Reyes, owner of Saltmarsh:
"Ines turned our bins into a larder. The best thing on the menu most weeks
started as something we used to throw away."

item.text:
I’d build this around **“The living larder”**: a portfolio that feels like stepping into your kitchen, with a 3D wall of preserving jars that changes as you scroll.

Your strongest story is what happens before service: turning trim into something valuable, building a larder of 40+ ferments, and passing that knowledge to apprentices. That gives the movement a purpose.

**Visual direction**

Warm off-white, ink-black typography, brine green and amber glass. Large editorial headlines alongside small handwritten-style labels and dates. Your food photography, larder labels and *Brine* drawings would give it a personal, tactile feel.

The main 3D element would be a carefully lit shelf of jars, surrounded by generous space. Avoid a conventional tech-portfolio look: the site should feel like a chef’s working notebook brought to life.

**The scroll journey**

1. **Opening — “Before service, everything is alive.”**  
   Your name, “Chef, fermenter, teacher. Leeds,” and a short introduction beside the jar wall. Scrolling gently brings the camera toward the shelf. A visible link lets visitors jump straight to your work.

2. **The larder — the centrepiece.**  
   Three jars become visual anchors for fermentation, whole-vegetable cooking and preservation. Labels appear as the shelf moves through view; selecting one reveals photography and a short story. Specific ingredients and processes would come from your material, rather than invented examples.

3. **Saltmarsh — what the work changes.**  
   The 3D scene settles into a photographic editorial layout: dishes, prep and kitchen details. Highlight the 40-seat restaurant, weekly-changing menu, 40+ rotating ferments and kitchen waste reduced from 14 kg to 5 kg per week. Include Callum’s recommendation.

4. **Passing it on.**  
   Apprentices, staff meal and your first-Monday workshops. Use a gently moving strip of photographs and notes, with workshop information easy to find. Bring in Sunday Pot as another expression of cooking for other people.

5. **Brine — a small reading table.**  
   Four issues arranged as overlapping covers that separate slightly on scroll. Each opens into an accessible reader, with selectable text alongside the scans. Credit Olu’s drawings.

6. **Roots and contact.**  
   Your grandmother’s ogiri pot offers a personal closing image, alongside a short account of your influences. Keep career history compact, and finish with clear contact links once those details are supplied.

**How the motion should work**

Use one memorable 3D sequence, then quieter image reveals and subtle layering. Keep normal scrolling, readable text and obvious navigation throughout. On mobile, simplify the scene; with reduced motion enabled, show a composed still image and the same complete content.

**Build approach, once approved**

Use Astro for a fast, content-led site, Three.js for the jar wall, and GSAP for the scroll choreography. Load the 3D scene after the opening content, compress images, and provide a static fallback. Verify keyboard access, mobile performance and reduced-motion behaviour before launch.

**Material to resolve before building**

- The folder contains two text files; the photos and scans are described but aren’t included yet.
- Your notes say you took over the kitchen in September 2022; LinkedIn dates the head-chef role to March 2022. Confirm how those dates relate before publishing.
- Confirm permission and credits for Priya’s photography and Olu’s drawings, plus contact details and the workshop enquiry route.

No files have been changed and nothing has been built.
